Person named ‘K’ from China paid five defendants to injure Huang Yi-hao, New Taipei prosecutors say

Taiwanese prosecutors have charged five men over a plot to ram a car into a comedian who made fun of the Chinese Communist party and Xi Jinping .

Taiwan has repeatedly accused China of transnational repression to silence critics on the self-governed island, which Beijing claims as its territory and has vowed to take by force if necessary.

In one performance, Huang Yi-hao insulted the Chinese leader’s appearance, compared him to Winnie-the-Pooh and tore into his political record.

Prosecutors in New Taipei said on Wednesday that an individual from mainland China who was identified as “K” had paid the five defendants to injure Huang badly enough to require hospitalisation.

The prosecutors said: “This case involves a serious incident in which the Chinese Communist party is suspected of using cross-border suppression tactics to direct lawless elements in our country to suppress dissenting political voices through extreme violence.”

China’s Taiwan Affairs Office did not respond to requests for comment.

A GPS tracker was allegedly put on Huang’s scooter months before the attack to identify his daily routines, Taiwan’s Central News Agency said. On 11 September, two defendants drove into Huang’s bike as he rode home, but stopped after hearing Huang scream, prosecutors said.

The comedian was left with a bruised pelvis and the suspects then allegedly pretended to help with an insurance claim in order to send a photo of Huang’s medical certificate to K.

K refused to pay the full sum of NT$450,000 (US$13,900; £10,370) promised to the suspects because Huang’s injuries were only minor, the statement said.

On Wednesday, Huang reposted a video from December 2025 in which he asked the audience to help him by shouting out the name of the person he was about to describe.

In a fast-paced diatribe, the comedian, dressed in a traditional gown, evoked “swept-back hair” and a “plump figure”, and criticised policies on Hong Kong, Covid and the property market. After finishing with an expletive, the crowd chanted back Xi’s name before breaking into applause.

In May, two people were prosecuted after spreading faeces and paint at a Taipei club hours before a Huang show.

Lev Nachman, a professor of political science at National Taiwan University, said: “It is important to remember that what we are reading about is obviously a more extreme case, but there have been threats and acts of violence against critics of the Communist party here in Taiwan for many years.”

Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council said in October that at least 126 individuals had been affected by Chinese transnational repression.

The Guardian has contacted the Chinese foreign ministry for comment.

In a post on Wednesday, Huang said: “If people can be subjected to this kind of treatment simply for criticising the Chinese Communist party when it does not even govern Taiwan, how can we expect to retain our current freedom of speech if the CCP were ever to rule Taiwan?”

In another post on Facebook, Huang said he would not cancel future performances but that he was “no hero”.

“I write it because it’s funny,” he said. “If I stop, it will only be because I’ve got bored of it.”

stories.title: EFF Launches Guide to Help Parents and Youth Protect Privacy Online
stories.summary: Guide Includes Easy, Quick Ways To Identify and Protect Against Online Threats SAN FRANCISCO – The Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) has published “ Online Privacy for Parents and Youth ,” a new guide to help families protect themselves online. "Parents don’t need to be technology experts to help their children navigate the digital world safely” said EFF Public Interest Technology Director Babette Ngene. “At EFF, we believe in empowering families with the knowledge and confidence to make informed decisions about their digital lives. It’s about meeting families where they are and giving parents the guidance they need to have meaningful conversations with their children about digital safety, based on what works best for their families.” EFF launches this crucial resource as state and local governments consider enacting well-meaning but ill-advised laws that cut young people off from essential information and experiences, particularly harming vulnerable youth and marginalized groups who often find safety in supportive online communities they can't access offline. Such laws also entail age gating, which compromises the privacy of all internet users and stifles young users’ ability to learn, grow, and express themselves. “Deciding how to help your young people use the internet—including engaging with video games, social media, web search, and everything else—is a complicated topic that touches on many different skillsets and ideas,” said EFF Senior Security and Privacy Activist Thorin Klosowski. “But ultimately it's up to families – not governments – to decide when and how to engage with these sorts of questions.” Each young person has unique needs, and, just like their wardrobe, that changes as they age. Parents can engage in thoughtful planning to find the best, most efficient solutions that evolve along with their children. EFF’s guide is about helping parents explore their concerns and identify the threats their children face – like trusting AI chatbots or sharing personal information with strangers – and then determine steps they and their children can take to mitigate those risks while still using the games, educational materials, and communication platforms that help them grow. The guide also compiles links to parental control setup documentation for a variety of popular devices and platforms, and advises parents on quick, easy tasks they can perform…

stories.title: Trump sued over Canadian tariffs in latest legal challenge
stories.summary: The lawsuit argues the White House exceeded its authority in imposing the latest tariffs on the country and caused "immediate harm to American businesses".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 20 October 2026

US President Donald Trump is facing another legal challenge on tariffs after the group that successfully sued over his so-called "liberation day" import taxes filed a new lawsuit over the latest Canadian levies.

The White House imposed a 50% levy on some $20bn of Canadian goods after trade talks between the US and Canada broke down in August.

The Liberty Justice Center filed a suit on behalf of US food business Gellert Global Group, urging the US Court of International Trade to find the levies unlawful and to order refunds with interest for affected importers.

The lawsuit argues the White House exceeded its authority in imposing the tariffs and caused "immediate harm to American businesses".

The White House has been contacted for comment.

Gellert Global Group is a third-generation family business that is paying 50% tariffs on cheese exported from Canada. The New Jersey-based firm is also facing retaliatory tariffs from Canada on American-made cheese it sells north of the border.

Co-chief executive Thomas Gellert said the firm had spent generations building relationships with suppliers and customers in the food industry.

"These tariffs disrupt those relationships overnight and create costs and uncertainty that ripple through the entire supply chain," he said on Tuesday.

The Liberty Justice Center is challenging the administration's use of Section 338 of the 1930 Tariff Act to hit Canadian goods from wine to dairy products and hockey sticks.

That section of the nearly 100-year-old Act is aimed at protecting US business against foreign discrimination, but the legal group is arguing that it does not allow the executive branch "to impose sweeping tariffs or import restrictions whenever a trade dispute arises".

The US-Canada trade war in 5 charts Published 31 August

The lawsuit seeks to challenge the White House's reliance on retaliatory tariffs imposed by Canada to justify its own duties under Section 338.

Canada has imposed a series of countermeasures against numerous US tariffs. Last month, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney matched the Section 338 US tariffs "dollar for dollar" after Trump imposed them for what he called "unequal treatment" of US cars, dairy and alcohol.

It also points out Section 338 requires a 30-day waiting period before levies can be imposed, but the tariff on products including cheese was added to the list just a week before tariff collection began.

Sara Albrecht, chief executive of the Liberty Justice Center, said the case was not about Trump himself but about the presidency.

"No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required," she said.

The lawsuit argues that Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 has been superseded by Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.

It also argues that if Section 338 still applies, the White House has not established the legal basis for the sweeping tariffs against Canada.

"The case is not an objection to tariffs as such. It asks who has the power to impose them and whether the executive branch followed the law Congress wrote," the Liberty Justice Center said.

The law group has also filed a motion for a preliminary injunction to block their collection.

It is the fourth case brought by the group against Trump's tariffs, including its successful case against the sweeping tariffs brought in under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) that were struck down in February this year.

Albrecht said the group had brought all the cases for the same reason: "the Constitution gives tariff power to Congress. The executive branch cannot keep moving the same policy from one statute to another and pretend the limits disappear".

Google Cloud outage: A summary

Time to recap…

A power outage at a Google Cloud data centre near London has caused serious failures to services today, affecting operations for several UK banks.

Problems were first detected just after 7am this morning, disrupting “multiple services” in Google’s europe-west2 region (London).

Google blamed the problem on a ‘power issue’ – just afternoon today it said this event had been mitigated. By 1pm UK time services were recovering, and at 3pm Google said services were back online for most customers, with only “a very small number” still affected.

But by that time, millions of customers had been left unable to access and send cash at banks including Lloyds, HSBC and Revolut .

Revolut said:

double quotation mark “We are currently experiencing a service disruption affecting multiple services. We can confirm that all our customers’ money and data are safe. We’ve been working to fix the issue since it was identified this morning and apologise to anyone affected and for any inconvenience caused.”

A spokesperson for Lloyds added:

double quotation mark “Our app is online and customers can log in normally, though we understand some are having issues with certain online services this morning. We are aware of similar issues affecting other organisations and are monitoring the situation closely.”

Legal proceedings were disrupted, because the video system used by defendants, lawyers and other parties to attend court hearings remotely across England and Wales which failed to work throughout the morning.

The City regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority , confirmed it was in touch with Google and seeking more information about the outage.

This outage will be the first major test for the FCA and Bank of England , since the City watchdogs were handed powers to regulate Google and other rival services that have been supplying “critical” cloud services to UK financial firms this summer.

Tech experts said the outage was another reminder of the dangers of relying on a small number of technology providers for cloud services, a year after problems at Amazon Cloud caused more widespread disruption.

Reynolds: Chinese EV decision will depend on UK interests

Business secretary Johnny Reynolds has insisted any decision to impose tariffs on Chinese EVs will be about British, not EU interests .

He told the business select committee that some were under the misapprehension that the EU wanted the UK to put tariffs on EVs because they feared the Chinese could use Britain as a “backdoor” to the bloc, circumventing trade defence measures including tariffs on EVs and quota on electric hybrid cars.

He point out that this Chinese cars exported from the UK “would not qualify” for duty free exports to the EU under the rules of origin clauses in the Brexit trade and cooperation agreement”.

He was also asked about last week’s Franco-German paper proposing that the UK would be included in the upcoming Made in Europe legislation on condition London aligned with EU trade defence measures.

But he said the “detail” of that proposal, which has yet to be adopted by the EU in any new drafting of the Industrial Accelerator Act, “has not been surfaced to the degree to which we’d be able to definitively say that that is what the ask is of the UK.”

Revolut said:

We’ve been working to fix the issue since it was identified this morning and apologise to anyone affected and for any inconvenience caused.”

double quotation mark “Our app is online and customers can log in normally, though we understand some are having issues with certain online services this morning. We are aware of similar issues affecting other organisations and are monitoring the situation closely.”

Tech experts said the outage was another reminder of the dangers of relying on a small number of technology providers for cloud services, a year after problems at Amazon Cloud caused more widespread disruption.

Google: We'll publish an analysis of what went wrong

Google add that it does not plan to provide further updates about the outage on its Service Health page – another sign that it thinks it has pretty much resolved the problem with its cloud services today.

It adds:

double quotation mark We will publish an analysis of this incident once we have completed our internal investigation. We thank you for your patience while we’re working on resolving the issue.

Google: issue has been mitigated for most customers

Newsflash: Google has declared that it has won, pretty much, its battle against today’s tech outage at its London-based cloud computing systems.

In an updated status message , Google says:

double quotation mark Multiple services were experiencing issues in the europe-west2 region.

The shift to the past tense is significant – until now, the messages said that services “are” experiencing issues.

Google then declares that all but a few customers have now been helped, saying:

double quotation mark The issue with impacted GCP products has been mitigated for most of the customers and it is believed to be affecting currently a very small number of customers and our Engineering Team is working on it. If you have questions or are impacted, please open a case with the Support Team and we will work with you until this issue is resolved.

Royal Mail has said it was aware of the issues caused to its services by the Google Cloud outage, and added that there was no effect on letter and parcel deliveries.

Not that those deliveries are always good enough!

Businesss secretary Johnny Reynolds has said he has summoned Royal Mail bosses in for talks to discuss changes to improve the services, my colleague Lisa O’Carroll reports.

He told a parliamentary business committee that the Royal Mail is not delivering “the level of service people expect”.

Royal Mail have not met their first or second class standards for almost 10 years, the committee heard.

Reynolds said the government had negotiated the take over by Czech billionaire Daniel Křetínský last year which included a curb on dividends “until performance improved”.

“I know for parliamentarians this in oral questions on Thursday and other correspondence with members of Parliament that it is one of the most significant issues they’re facing,” Reynolds told the committee.

He said the government “recognised the need for regulatory reform” but Ofcom was taking a lead at the moment on this subject.

double quotation mark “I am going to have Royal Mail and the unions in for a conversation about this. I need to respond to what MPs are being told. “Royal Mail is a really important institution and business, and I know it has significant ramifications when it’s not hitting the levels of service. And I can promise you, chair, whether it’s work with Ofcom, whether it’s work with, with, you know, any part, any key player, any stakeholder in this, we will do what we can to make sure Royal Mail is the service it needs to be.”

Lloyds: expect services to get back to normal soon

Lloyds Banking Group, which includes Halifax, is hopeful that services will be restored soon.

A spokesperson for Lloyds tells us:

double quotation mark “We understand the root issues have been resolved, so we expect to all our services back to normal soon.”

UK regulators want answers from Google about Cloud outage

The Financial Conduct Authority and Bank of England are pushing Google for details of today’s cloud services outage, as they face their first major test as new regulators of “critical” tech suppliers to UK banks.

Both the FCA and Bank of England were handed powers in July to start directly overseeing the local arms of Google Cloud and three other Silicon Valley rivals - Amazon Web Services, Oracle and Microsoft – after being designated as critical third parties by the UK government, as their services become a crucial part of increasingly digital banking services.

A spokesperson for the FCA said they were in touch with Google and seeking more information about the outage. The Bank of England’s Prudential Regulation Authority is also understood to be speaking with the tech firm about the service outage which began this morning ( details start here ).

The watchdogs are in charge of ensuring that the cloud providers are resilient and actively reducing the risk of cyber-attacks and major outages like the one experienced today, which has disrupted services for millions of people and businesses across the UK.

For its part, Google is meant to prove it is carrying out proper stress testing, including how it would respond to imagined emergency scenarios that would put their operations under severe strain. They’re also meant to have reported any major incidents, including this power outages, to the two regulators (though it’s unclear in what time frame).

Low-paid workers and hospitality firms face disruption

The failure of banking apps due to the Google Cloud outage could disproportionately affect those most struggling with the cost of living, argues audit, tax and business advisory firm Blick Rothenberg .

Blick Rothenberg partner Andrew Sanford explains:

double quotation mark “Weekly or fortnightly paid employees, often those on lower wages, may have found that they are unable to access their funds on the very day where they have payments or commitments to make.” “The hospitality sector will also be disproportionately impacted by those people affected by the outage with no means of making payment, who simply do not go the pub or restaurant.”

Affected companies coming back online again

There are signs that the companies affected by Google’s outage are getting online again.

Emma , the personal finance, budgeting, and money management app which was taken down by the Google Cloud outage ( see 10.11am ), has posted on X that it is operating again.

Emma says:

double quotation mark We’re back ✅ Emma is up and running again after this morning’s Google Cloud power outage in London . Your data and money were safe throughout. Some balances may take a little while to refresh. Thanks for your patience 💜

Google: We are seeing the recovery of services for most workloads

Newsflash: Google says service ​are being ‌restored ‌in its London-based ‌cloud region after today’s outage.

The company says:

double quotation mark “We are seeing the recovery of services for most workloads in europe-west2.”

This isn’t the end of the story, though – Google are promising another update by 3pm UK time.

Google added that they will provide an update by 06:00 PDT (2pm BST) with “current details” of the situation.

Google: The power event is mitigated

Newsflash: Google says the ‘power event’ which affected its London-based cloud computing operating and caused widepread disruption to services in the UK has been ‘mitigated’.

In a new statement on its Service Health page, Google reports seeing signs that services are being restored.

It says:

double quotation mark A power event caused an outage within europe-west2-b zone. The power event is mitigated. We are seeing the recovery of services and are prioritizing the recovery of existing workloads.Customers may not be able to yet create new workloads. Full recovery of existing workloads should be completed, tentatively by Tuesday, 2026-10-20 06:00 [Pacific Daylight Time].

[ CORRECTED: 6am PDT is 2pm UK time.]

The Google Cloud outage could result in some companies losing sales, and they might struggle to get much compensation, suggests Ryan Gracey , partner at law firm Gordons.

double quotation mark “Many businesses will be discovering today that their cloud contracts protect the supplier far more than they protect the customer. “When a provider goes down, the usual remedy is a modest credit against future fees. That is small consolation set against lost revenue, frustrated customers and damage to reputation. “Liability for those wider losses is typically capped or excluded altogether. The real exposure sits in the gap between how heavily a business depends on its provider and how little its contract actually guarantees. For banks, the stakes are higher still. Regulators expect them to keep essential services running even when a key supplier fails. “Outsourcing a service does not mean outsourcing responsibility for it. Boards should be asking, not just what their contracts promise, but whether the business could keep going if its provider went dark for a day.”

Google: power event disrupted our Cloud services

Google are blaming a ‘power event’ for the disruption at its London-based Cloud computing operations today.

In an update on its status page, Google says:

double quotation mark Due to a power event we had suffered an outage within europe-west2-b zone. The power event is mitigated. Partial mitigation to infrastructure services will be observed within the next 30 minutes and the remaining services will be mitigated there after.

PA: Court hearings delayed as nationwide video system goes down

The video system used by courts across England and Wales went down on Tuesday in an issue believed to be linked to the wider Google outage, the Press Association report.

The Cloud Video Platform (CVP), which is used by defendants, lawyers and other parties to attend court hearings remotely, was not functioning throughout the morning.

Users expecting to attend court on video link were met with a message saying there was an internal server error.

The issue is expected to have left many hearings across the country delayed or unable to go ahead as the system is often used for defendants who are in custody to attend court.

The judge in the Russell Brand trial, Mr Justice Bennathan, decided to press on with proceedings at Southwark Crown Court on Tuesday morning despite the link being broken.

Some journalists who would have been watching online were squeezed into extra seats in court, but many were not able to follow the proceedings as the fourth complainant started her evidence.

Staff at the court said there was a national outage and did not know when it would be resolved.

It is understood to be linked to an outage affecting Google’s Cloud network, which affected businesses including online bank Revolut , delivery service DPD and Royal Mail.

The nature of cloud ecosystems mean that a problem in one region can ripple out and cause widesread disruption.

Dr Amro Al-Said Ahmad , lecturer in computer science at Keele University , explains:

double quotation mark “Another outage, another reminder of the fragility of cloud infrastructure. Google Cloud is currently experiencing a major incident affecting the europe-west2 (London) region, with elevated errors and intermittent network failures impacting more than 38 cloud-native services across key categories including Compute & Containers, Storage & Databases, Analytics & Data Processing, Networking & Connectivity, Messaging & Streaming, Caching & Memory Services, and AI/Platform Services. “Google Engineers are actively investigating the issue and testing mitigations, including moving impacted workloads to alternative regions where feasible. The disruption has also affected several major organisations and financial institutions that rely on the affected region. “More importantly, the incident highlights the dependency effect of modern cloud ecosystems. When a core cloud region experiences failures, the impact extends far beyond the directly affected services. Applications, APIs, databases, authentication systems, payment platforms, analytics pipelines, and third-party SaaS products that depend on those services can all experience cascading failures. “A problem in a single cloud region can therefore propagate through an entire digital supply chain, affecting organisations that are several layers removed from the original outage. While this is a regional outage centred on europe-west2, the breadth of affected services highlights a key cloud engineering lesson: resilience is not achieved by simply moving to the cloud. True resilience requires designing for regional failures through multi-region deployments, workload portability, and tested disaster recovery procedures.”

A Lloyds spokesperson has confirmed the bank (which includes Halifax) has experienced problems today:

double quotation mark “Our app is online and customers can log in normally, though we understand some are having issues with certain online services this morning. We are aware of similar issues affecting other organisations and are monitoring the situation closely.”

Google’s latest update on its Cloud outage reiterates what we knew already.

It says:

double quotation mark We apologize to all who are affected by the disruption. Symptoms Multiple Google Cloud services are experiencing elevated errors and intermittent network failures in europe-west2 region. Note: Looker Studio is not impacted by this outage. Workaround If feasible, the impacted customer may try to migrate their workload impacted to another available location (zone or region).

stories.title: TP-Link tries to appease Trump admin with pledge to assemble routers in US
stories.summary: TP-Link can't sell latest routers in US despite rivals getting FCC approvals.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
TP-Link can’t sell latest routers in US despite rivals getting FCC approvals.

TP-Link yesterday announced plans to assemble Wi-Fi routers in the US, as the company attempts to get the Trump administration’s approval to sell its newest routers to American consumers.

The timing is uncertain, as TP-Link’s press release said it expects US-based assembly to begin “as early as” 2027. TP-Link’s application to sell new routers in the US could be rejected by the Trump administration or remain pending long enough to push the US-based assembly to 2028.

“Pending US regulatory approval, TP-Link expects domestic assembly of its groundbreaking Wi-Fi 8 home networking product line to begin as early as next year,” the company said. TP-Link said it signed a Letter of Intent with US company Keytronic, which agreed “to become a primary domestic manufacturing partner for TP-Link, supporting assembly of the company’s advanced networking portfolio in Corinth, Mississippi.”

TP-Link can’t sell its Wi-Fi 8 routers in the US because of the Federal Communications Commission ban on consumer-grade routers produced wholly or partly in other countries. Previous TP-Link routers that were already approved for import and sale are still available.

What counts as a US router is unclear

The FCC has given exemptions to a number of prominent router makers, but TP-Link’s history as a Chinese company is making it difficult to obtain FCC clearance. Founded in China in 1996, TP-Link moved its headquarters to California in October 2024. It says that “TP-Link Systems devices sold in the US are manufactured in Vietnam and TP-Link Systems is an independent, US company that is not owned or controlled by any foreign government.”

While TP-Link assembles routers in Vietnam, most of the components are reportedly imported from China. TP-Link’s plan to assemble routers in the US will still require it to import components, but the company hopes investment in the US will help it gain the Trump administration’s favor.

While the FCC is urging router makers to move more of their operations to the US, a TP-Link official said the government has provided no clear guidance on how much US manufacturing is enough to obtain an exemption from the foreign router ban.

“There are no published guidelines that say, ‘Well, it could be 25 percent US, or it could be 15 percent US,'” TP-Link corporate affairs officer Steve Kovsky told PCMag . Kovsky said that many components “are just not available from a domestic source, and this is not a TP-Link issue. This is an issue for all manufacturers that are trying to onshore manufacturing.”

In a letter to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr and the agency’s commissioners last week, Kovsky said TP-Link is proposing “a nearly $1 billion investment in America that would result in equipping existing US factories, and ultimately building new, highly automated manufacturing facilities, to start assembling next-generation Wi-Fi 8 routers in the United States as soon as next year, creating hundreds of new jobs.”

TP-Link struggles to convince Trump admin

TP-Link’s letter said it will make the proposed investment if it receives approval to sell Wi-Fi 8 routers in the US. “This investment would build upon TP-Link’s existing US footprint, which includes a global headquarters in Irvine, Calif., and more than 700 US employees,” TP-Link told the FCC. “As part of this investment, TP-Link would begin assembling these Wi-Fi 8 devices in the United States by next year, and the devices will incorporate software and firmware developed, written, and stored in the United States by TP-Link’s US engineering organization.”

The FCC isn’t the only agency that TP-Link has to convince. The FCC process for issuing exemptions from the ban requires each router maker to first obtain a determination from the Department of Defense or Department of Homeland Security that its devices do not pose national security risks.

Router makers that received exemptions so far include Netgear, Asus, Adtran, Amazon and its Eero subsidiary, Calix, Nokia, SpaceX’s Starlink division, and others. TP-Link urged the Trump administration to ensure that its “reviewers fairly apply the same consistent review standards to TP-Link as have been applied to all other applicants.”

TP-Link’s 2024 move to the US came amid investigations into high-profile attacks linked to the Chinese government, including a botnet composed mostly of TP-Link routers. The Russian GRU also compromised TP-Link routers to steal information, US intelligence agencies said in April 2026 .

TP-Link is far from the only router maker with security problems. For example, so-called AirSnitch attacks described in research this year were reported to work on routers made by Netgear, D-Link, Ubiquiti, Cisco, and those running DD-WRT and OpenWrt.

Republican AGs urge FCC to stand firm

TP-Link’s letter to the FCC last week said its application for an exemption provides “complete responses” to questions about its corporate structure and manufacturing and supply chain.

“TP-Link prioritizes the security of US consumer networking data; user data processed by TP-Link’s US products is encrypted and housed on Amazon Web Services infrastructure in Virginia,” the company said. “And of course, TP-Link does not, and will not, share customer network data with foreign governments or unauthorized third parties.”

TP-Link also faces opposition from Republican state attorneys general. The AGs from Florida, Montana, Iowa, and Nebraska sued TP-Link this month , alleging that it lied to consumers about its connections to China and the risks of its routers being exploited by Chinese state hackers.

A group of 21 Republican state AGs then sent a letter to the FCC questioning TP-Link’s claims regarding router security and the company’s independence from China. The letter urged the FCC to require remedies for “past and ongoing state-law violations” in its review of TP-Link’s application and to protect router users “from exploitation by the Chinese Communist Party.”

stories.title: Does anyone actually want to win the medium-lift race in the United States?
stories.summary: Ars Technica is here to help with a guide to the medium-lift space race.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Ars Technica is here to help with a guide to the medium-lift space race.

It has been 13 years since the debut of a new medium-lift rocket in the United States, the Antares vehicle developed by Orbital Sciences Corporation.

The initial 100-series variant of the Antares rocket was kind of a hot mess. The rocket used old Soviet engines built during the era when Apollo astronauts were landing on the Moon. Decades later, in the 1990s, Aerojet acquired the engines and refurbished them for a rocket that would launch in the 2010s. Predictably, on the fifth launch of an Antares rocket in 2014, it exploded.

The Antares vehicle is the last of a dying breed of medium-lift rockets—defined as having a lift capacity of 2 to 20 metric tons—in the United States. Nearly a decade and a half later there is a new generation of medium-lift vehicles coming online, and they are starkly different from Antares, which had not just Russian engines but a core stage manufactured in Ukraine.

Four forthcoming rockets all have engines built by the rocket’s manufacturer in the United States. Each of these companies has taken various lessons from SpaceX’s successful Falcon 9 rocket, arguably the most important of which is to build as much of one’s rocket, and particularly the engines, in-house as possible to control timelines and costs.

Now, with SpaceX pulling the Falcon 9 rocket from the commercial market as soon as 2028, the “race” to bring new medium-lift capacity into service is for more than bragging rights. There are fortunes to be made, and commercial space startups to be saved.

Satellite operators legitimately don’t know who to book launches with in the 2027 to 2030 timeframe because of uncertainty over which rockets will be available. The Falcon 9 is no longer for sale. The larger Vulcan and New Glenn rockets have stacked manifests and are expensive for small- and medium-sized satellites. And no one really knows which new medium-lift vehicles will be ready and capable of scaling up their launch cadence.

With all of this in mind, Ars Technica is here to help with a guide to the medium-lift space race in the United States, along with some (almost certainly wrong) predictions on when the rockets may debut. The list below is in our expected order of launch. Disagree? Feel free to shame us in the comments. And if you’re an engineer or technician working on one of these projects, keep going. This stuff is really hard and we salute your dedication. Prove us wrong!

Stoke Space: Nova

The smallest of the medium-lift rockets under development, with a capacity of 3 tons in fully reusable mode and 7 tons in expendable mode, the Nova rocket is also arguably the most ambitious.

That’s because the rocket aims for full reusability, with a novel upper stage thruster design and heat shield to solve the difficult problem of protecting a vehicle reentering at orbital velocity. Additionally, the first-stage engines are full-flow staged combustion, which is ambitious for a first engine design.

Despite all of this, the rocket is making credible progress toward liftoff. The Nova rocket’s first stage is nearly complete at its factory in Kent, Washington. Last week Stoke shipped the second stage of Nova to its test site, and if hot-fire tests are successful it will move to the launch site. The launch complex at Cape Canaveral, Florida, is nearly complete.

Recently, for the first time, Stoke began to publicly talk about a date for Nova’s debut. The company is targeting “early” 2027 for launch. That’s probably optimistic, but we could see a late spring or summer debut.

Predicted launch debut : July 2027

Relativity Space: Terran R

Technically, this is not a medium-lift rocket. The company is advertising up to 33.5 metric tons to low-Earth orbit in fully expendable mode for Terran R. But new rockets rarely hit their advertised lift capacity early in their lifetime, and with a reusable first stage (which is necessary for the economics of Terran R to close), the lift capacity is closer to 20 metric tons.

Nevertheless, this is a large and ambitious project. And it was pretty much left for dead until former Google Chief Executive Eric Schmidt acquired the company a year and a half ago. Schmidt has injected much-needed funding into Relativity, and sources report that morale at the Long Beach, California-based company has improved significantly.

In recent months the company has reported some notable progress. It completed acceptance testing for all 13 of the Aeon R engines that will power its first stage, qualified the first stage structures, and is making progress on assembly of the first stage. Then, last Friday, the company said the Terran R’s second stage had successfully completed its first integrated hot fire test.

Stoke and Relativity are fairly close to one another in their development timelines. Relativity is ahead in second stage testing, but Stoke has a lead in launch site readiness. I am going to give the slight edge to the smaller rocket in terms of being ready for launch.

Predicted launch debut : September 2027

Rocket Lab: Neutron

With a lift capacity of between 8.5 and 15 metric tons, depending on first stage reuse and landing site, Rocket Lab’s Neutron rocket slots somewhere in between Nova and Terran R.

For a long time it appeared as though Neutron would become the first new medium-lift rocket to debut since Antares, but the vehicle has had some teething pains: Rocket Lab has experienced some problems with the Archimedes engine , and more recently the company revealed some challenges with carbon-fiber domes.

The Neutron rocket’s first stage is the “largest pressurized structure ever made out of carbon composite,” Rocket Lab chief Peter Beck said this month. “Because of its scale, we’ve had to develop new out-of-autoclave processes to build Neutron, and this includes custom cure cycles for the very large pieces, like the forward and aft domes for the propellant tanks on Stage One.”

That doesn’t sound particularly easy. Given the lack of flight hardware in evidence, we’re not sure the company meets its latest launch target, which is now sometime in 2027.

Predicted launch debut : January 2028

Firefly/Northrop Grumman: Eclipse

We began this article with the Antares rocket, which was developed by Orbital Sciences. That company was later acquired by Northrop Grumman. A few years ago, seeking a home-grown alternative to Antares, Northrop announced a partnership with Firefly to co-develop the Eclipse rocket .

Firefly is developing the Miranda engines that will power Eclipse’s first stage, and this work appears to be progressing well. But there has been little public talk about development of the first and second stage hardware that will be built around the Miranda engine. Similar to Rocket Lab, Firefly and Northrop are also working with carbon-composite structures, so there may be some challenges there.

The partnership between Firefly, a new space company, and Northrop, a traditional space company, is also likely to produce some friction. It is difficult to make an educated guess on Eclipse because there is so much uncertainty about the rocket’s development. Typically, that means things aren’t going well or quickly. For now, we’re leaning toward pessimism.

Predicted launch debut : NET 2029

stories.title: 'Mindset shift' needed within government on No10 North, says deputy
stories.summary: Number 10 North deputy director Duncan Parish has told a conference he is still facing "institutional barriers".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham opened Number 10 North in July

Published 3 hours ago

A "mindset shift" is needed across the UK's central government to help Number 10 North deliver its objectives, its deputy director has said.

Duncan Parish told a conference in Lincolnshire on Wednesday there were "institutional challenges" within government that needed to be overcome to deliver change.

The Manchester office of Number 10 North - sister to London's Downing Street - was set up by Prime Minister Andy Burnham in July.

Burnham's political opponents have called the office a "gimmick" and raised transparency concerns about the costs involved.

Speaking to the Great Exhibition conference of local political and business leaders, Parish said his career in the civil service to date had "not been without its frustrations" and there can be "friction" between different parts of government which have "similar but ever so slightly competing objectives".

Parish, a civil servant in Whitehall before moving to Manchester four years ago, said Number 10 North staff were "delivering outcomes at a national level across a huge range of areas" including health, transport, education and social care.

"But we continually need to work to overcome those institutional challenges," he added.

He said one priority of Number 10 North was to "shift power and accountability" closer to local areas, but acknowledged "that means reforming the civil service as well" - by not viewing national, regional and local government as separate.

Duncan Parish spoke to local political and business leaders in Lincolnshire, in an event chaired by regional mayor Dame Andrea Jenkyns

Describing Number 10 North's second focus of growth, Parish told local leaders: "We're here to unblock issues that may have become stalled or where boundaries within government end up being a hindrance."

He said that "too often, working within government or departments can be perceived as either difficult or slow".

"But to deliver that change, requires us all to change - and part of that change is a mindset shift within central government," he said.

"We need to focus on the whole country and work across those boundaries, bringing in mayoral strategic authorities like Greater Lincolnshire into discussions that previously they may not have been part of - working bottom-up, rather than top-down."

His comments come as the government continues to face questions about the cost to the taxpayer of the new headquarters.

Few figures released

In September, Conservative shadow minister Mike Wood raised concerns about "little information and so little transparency" surrounding Number 10 North which he described as a "gimmick".

"The minister either doesn't know or won't tell us how much No 10 North will cost, how many people work there or how many of them actually turn up to work - it's almost as though this hasn't been properly thought through," he told a House of Commons debate.

He called for the annual budget, staff levels and office attendance statistics to be published. Current staffing levels have also not yet been clarified.

Cabinet Office minister Sally Jameson said last week that the government did not know how much has been spent on hotels for No 10 North staff, ministers and special advisers travelling between London and Manchester since it opened.

The cost is "not centrally collated" but is "being met within existing departmental budgets", Jameson said in response to a parliamentary question.

Number 10 North's latest summit of regional mayors, held in its "situation room", will take place on Thursday. Burnham has previously indicated he will work there at least once a week, and hosted the Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin in September .

Parish added in his speech: "How will we know if Number 10 North is working?

"Ultimately, success will be in people in the UK feeling the difference in their communities, with greater opportunities, improved living standards, faster decisions...more joined up services and a stronger voices in the future of their place."

Use of tools ‘may result in the transfer of sensitive data’ to China, defense department says

The US government on Monday ordered its agencies to stop using artificial intelligence (AI) tools from the Chinese startup DeepSeek , as the countries race for dominance in the fast-moving sector.

A notice from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced the ban on products developed by DeepSeek – and tools created using DeepSeek by third parties – saying they must be removed from IT devices.

The DHS can issue direction to civilian agencies but not the military or intelligence services. The US defense department did not respond to an AFP request for comment.

“DeepSeek’s models present multiple threat vectors,” said a document attached to Monday’s notice.

Use of DeepSeek AI tools “may result in the transfer of sensitive data to [China] if used by US government employees or vendors”, the department warned.

Its servers are located in China, where the legal system permits the government “extensive authority” to access private company infrastructure, it said.

DeepSeek has been contacted for comment.

One of China’s top AI labs, DeepSeek shook up the industry in January 2025 with a low-cost, high-performance chatbot, challenging assumptions of US dominance.

The firm released a long-awaited new model, V4, in April, and earlier in October updated a faster, more lightweight version of V4.

The US has accused DeepSeek and other top Chinese AI firms of systematically stealing the capabilities of cutting-edge models developed by American rivals.

Despite their fierce competition in the field, when their leaders Xi Jinping and Donald Trump met at the White House in September, China and the US agreed to set up a “communication channel” for AI incidents.

The topic is expected to arise again at a meeting between Xi and Trump at a summit scheduled for November in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.

stories.title: Victory! Court Rules OPM Data Disclosure to DOGE Is Unlawful
stories.summary: In a victory for data privacy, a federal court in New York definitively ruled that the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) violated the law when it disclosed millions of federal employee records to DOGE agents. In a summary judgment ruling issued on October 20, 2026, the court found that OPM violated two provisions of the Privacy Act—one restricting disclosure of personal records between agencies and another requiring agencies to protect the security and confidentiality of records. Since the case was filed, many DOGE agents have left the government and OPM has rescinded their database access. However, OPM should still clean up the cybersecurity mess it created. The court will decide the remedy at a later date. "By virtue of the Court’s summary judgment ruling, OPM’s decision to grant DOGE Agents broad access to its systems of recordings containing [personally identifiable information (PII)] has been held unlawful," Judge Denise Cote wrote. "The record also provides no support for a finding that it was the pursuit of a modernization agenda that prompted OPM to grant sweeping and expedited access to a score of DOGE Agents to its systems of records containing PII," she added. OPM maintains databases of highly sensitive personal information about tens of millions of federal employees, retirees, and job applicants. Starting in January 2025, OPM disclosed data to the U.S. DOGE Service, initially led by Elon Musk. This disclosure violates the federal Privacy Act of 1974, a watershed anti-surveillance statute that prevents the federal government from abusing our personal information. EFF sued OPM and DOGE because this data disclosure violates the Privacy Act. We represent unions of federal employees – the American Federation of Government Employees and the Association of Administrative Law Judges – and individual employees. We seek injunctive and declaratory relief. We filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York. Our co-counsel are Lex Lumina LLP , State Democracy Defenders Fund , and The Chandra Law Firm LLC . stories.title: ‘I’m always being real’: what on earth persuades disgraced people like Elizabeth Holmes to let the cameras in?
stories.summary: With You Can See Everything, Holmes joins other such high-profile subjects as Lance Armstrong, Imelda Marcos and Anthony Weiner to allow film-makers to document their lives. But do they ever come out well? In You Can See Everything, convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes invites film-makers Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim into her home in a supposed act of “radical transparency”. Holmes is filmed, along with her partner, Billy Evans, and their two young children, in the weeks before starting a prison sentence for defrauding Theranos investors. “The best way for people to see who she is,” Evans says, “is to give as much access as possible into our daily lives”. It may also be the best way to market “Theranos 2.0”, which the couple are working on during filming. But the documentary questions whether Holmes is presenting her authentic self or a manufactured persona. Fielder speaks for the audience when he asks Holmes in a tense exchange whether she’s “being real” with him. “I’m always being real,” she says. That question of authenticity is at the heart of documentary film-making. You Can See Everything is as much about the ambiguous relationship between film-maker and subject as it is about Holmes herself. There is often a power struggle over narrative control in documentaries, with both sides of the dynamic wanting different outcomes from the final film. Watching You Can See Everything inevitably prompts the question: why would Holmes, days before she heads to jail, invite the scrutiny of a film crew? Continue reading...

stories.body:
These yachts are highly popular with the ‘super-bourgeoisie’ – and getting bigger. Can anything be done to stop them destroying our seas?

W ho knew? Apparently everyone did, apart from me: you don’t wear shoes on a superyacht. Now, about to step on to my first teak deck at the Monaco Yacht Show, I’ve got to take my trainers off, and I’m having a sock panic. Have they got holes? Do they even match? Do they smell?

To be honest, I’ve come dressed all wrong for Europe’s big annual superyacht trade exhibition. The code for men seems to be crisp and tucked in, blazers and chinos, navy and white, sculpted hair and designer sunnies. (I went colourful, loose, casual). For women, it’s something like Riviera elegance. Everyone – whether they’re Italian, French, English, German, American, exhibitors, buyers, brokers, charterers – seems to know each other. The international superyacht community seems to be a close-knit one, and I’m not part of it. Yet.

For now, though, I’m boarding my first vessel: a relatively modest Zeelander 8 – 23.9 metres (79ft) long, built in the Netherlands. It has a rather retro look about it, with pleasing curves and a rear end not unlike a Porsche’s. I could imagine James Bond at the wheel. It’s fast too, reaching 40 knots (46mph); I could be in Saint-Tropez in a little over an hour.

Downstairs there’s a huge owner’s cabin, plus a couple of double guest cabins, all en suite, with lots of nice details, such as a cream-coloured leather floor. In the less opulent crew quarters, there’s room for two or three. How much does it cost? This one is not actually for sale – some of the boats here are, others are for charter, some just for show. But I could order one just like it, it would take a year and a half to build and cost me about €9.5m (£8m).

Tempting, certainly, but I need to see a few more before rushing into anything. I can’t help noticing that, compared with some of the others packed into Port Hercules, the Zeelander 8 is a bit … well, small. Is it even a superyacht? There seems to be some debate about how long a yacht has to be to be super – some say 24 metres, others 30.

No question about this one – a Fast50, made by Italian builders Baglietto, with room for 12 guests and a crew of nine. It’s not as fast as the Dutch one, despite the name. Its four engines take it to 30 knots, but that’s actually very quick for a 50 metre boat. Perhaps more importantly, its gross tonnage, referring to internal volume, is 499; a sub-500GT yacht isn’t subject to the more stringent safety and environmental rules under the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) that yachts over 500GT are, so they require less frequent surveys and have fewer restrictions on crew size and certification. My favourite features are the large “beach club” (the open deck at the back) and the Jacuzzi right up at the pointy end. Imagine it: sitting with a glass of fizz, in the bubbles, at 30 knots, Céline Dion blasting out … where do I sign?

Oh, again. Not for sale. The first Fast50, fresh from the shipyard, is already sold, but they won’t tell me how much for or who to (superyacht owners can be quite shy). The search continues.

The trouble with superyachting, I’m finding here in Monaco, is that you think you’ve found the perfect vessel, and then you look over there and there’s a bigger, better one. It’s not just me – this is reflected in the Global Order Book, published by Boat International, which tracks construction projects. The 2026 GOB counts the number of yachts over 24 metres under construction globally at 1,093. In 2016, it counted 755 vessels under construction. This year’s figure is actually down 3.95% from last year, but that’s balanced by an increase in average length and gross tonnage. In other words, a few fewer, but they’re getting bigger. New prefixes are required, “mega” and “giga”, but for simplicity’s sake we’ll stick with superyacht. Here at MYS 2026 there are 118 superyachts, with a combined length of 5,508 metres, and a value of €4.5bn.

Despite the sock shame, I’m beginning to feel more comfortable. Most people are friendly. It’s a lovely day on the Côte d’Azur – I’m offered ice-cream, branded fans and straw hats. It’s not just the yachts, there are stands for everything connected. Would I like to come to a wine tasting later “exploring superyacht wine trends”? Of course I would. Am I interested in yachting in Saudi Arabia? Hmmm, maybe next year. There are loads of toys on show – jetskis, eFoils, even submersibles. And if you’re still finding life at sea boring, there’s a portable golf simulator, with cameras and sensors, plus a screen, with hundreds of real courses programmed into it. So after dropping anchor off St Barts you can play a round at St Andrews. It costs €170,000 (£143,000).

And so on to Nixie, built by Lürssen in Germany, owned by co-founder and CEO of Revolut, Nik Storonsky: 102 metres long, with a helipad, glass-bottomed infinity pool, dedicated spa and wellness zone, and a crew of 34, one of whom is busy polishing a stainless steel cleat on the lowest of its decks. Access, though, is “reserved exclusively for direct, potential clients,” says the Lürssen PR. Perhaps they think the average Guardian reader is not in the market to rent a boat the length of a football pitch. Nixie costs €2.4m a week to hire. A lot, I know, but if you split it between the 12 of you …

Anyway, it’s not even the biggest here, which I will be allowed on. First though I pass another – Boardwalk V, only 76.5 metres long and five years old, but this one is for sale, at a discount price! Down €14m, to just €135m. Not including the helicopter. Boardwalk V … it’s ringing a bell. Got it! And now the twin flags on the helicopter’s tail – the American stars and stripes and the tricolore of Italy – make sense. This boat belongs to Tilman Fertitta, billionaire owner of restaurants, hotels, casinos, and the Houston Rockets basketball team, and now Donald Trump’s ambassador to Italy. He made the news in June when hundreds came out to protest after he parked his brand new 117-metre yacht (also named Boardwalk, but without the V) in Venice. He’s got an upgrade – that’s why he’s selling this one.

To be honest there are some proper horrors on show. This one looks like a supersized 80s caravan, that one more like a bridge than a boat, another is bright red – like some kind of firefighting ship. “I don’t understand the clients,” says Rick. “They just want something that’s big and flashy and comfortable, they don’t care about anything else.” Rick is also pretty disparaging about the people who sell these boats, the brokers. “They’re like real estate agents, they say: ‘Look at the master cabin, look at all the light, the big windows,’ it’s all about the interior space.”

Guess what Rick does? Yup, yacht broker. It’s why we’ve changed his name. He also points out something about the way they look. “I don’t know if you’ve heard the analogy, but they look like irons.” As in electric irons, to do the ironing with, and oh my God, he’s so right – that shape, pointy at the bow, then rising and widening as you go aft, with a squared off swim platform … As Rick says, “once you see it, you can’t unsee it.”

I n a 2024 study , Oxfam identified 23 superyachts owned by 18 billionaires and estimated the average annual carbon footprint of each of these yachts to be 5,672 tonnes. For an average citizen of the world it would take 860 years to produce the same amount.

Oxfam zoomed in further to one family, the Waltons, heirs of the Walmart chain and owners of three superyachts (at this level you’re not talking about the haves and the have-yachts, you’re talking about the have-yachts and the have-lots-of-yachts). They travelled 56,000 nautical miles in a year with a combined carbon footprint of 18,000 tonnes. That’s equivalent to the carbon emissions of about 1,700 Walmart employees.

Superyachts use an awful lot of fuel – some of the bigger ones use more than 500 litres of diesel per hour , releasing CO 2 as well as nitrogen oxides and sulphur dioxide into the atmosphere. The recreational boating sector as a whole – including yachts – produces about 16m tonnes of CO 2 annually . It’s not just when they’re going along; at anchor they operate onboard generators to run their “hotel loads” (for air conditioning, stabilisation systems, lighting, galleys, hot tubs, etc) which emit further CO 2 . In addition, the vessels’ big anchors and chains act like the grim reaper’s scythe on the Posidonia seagrass which grows on the Mediterranean seabed and is a vital habitat for sea life as well as a source of oxygen.

And there are more and more of them. The big increases came in 2022 and 2023 when, as Boat International puts it, “orders soared as UHNWIs sought private holiday cocoons.” UHNWIs, you’ll know, are ultra-high net worth individuals, but why the big boom? Because a superyacht is “the best way to practise social distancing in a very safe and very comfortable way,” says Grégory Salle. Covid was brilliant for the superyacht sector, in other words. Salle is talking to me by video from Lille where he works at the French National Centre for Scientific Research. He’s also author of the thoroughly researched and surprisingly entertaining book Superyachts: Luxury, Tranquility and Ecocide, which has a whole chapter devoted to Posidonia seagrass.

Ecocide is not the superyacht’s only crime. “It has really become the symbol of excessive, unjustifiable wealth,” Salle says. Even though the gap between most of us and the people who have them is virtually unfathomable, “it looks like provocation, especially when all you’re hearing and reading about is crisis, austerity, poverty – including child poverty.”

Superyachts are also a kind of floating paradox that Salle calls “conspicuous seclusion. On the one hand they’re meant to be noticed, they’re massive, you can’t miss them. But at the same time the interior is hidden and of course it can sail away and escape ordinary people.”

Salle uses words and phrases such as “plutocracy”, “oligarchy” and the new “global super-bourgeoisie” about the people who own them, a “transnational capitalist class” who operate outside and above borders and rules. Look at the stern of the superyachts, under the name, and they’re almost all registered in places such as the Cayman Islands, the Marshall Islands, the Isle of Man and Malta – flag states offering, among other benefits, tax neutrality.

It’s hard to hide a superyacht, or ownership of one. We know about Mark Zuckerberg’s 118-metre Launchpad, and Jeff Bezos’s 127-metre Koru, estimated to have cost €444m. Koru caused a stir in 2022, when a historic bridge in Rotterdam, a Dutch national monument, was going to be dismantled in order to let it through. After the uproar its masts were stepped downstream in the end. Koru is actually a sailing yacht, which might sound like a greener way of doing it, but then Bezos also has a 75-metre support vessel, with additional crew accommodation, helipad, submarine, speedboats and cars, that follows Koru around like a loyal dog. Zuckerberg’s got a couple of support vessels too.

Roman Abramovich is another big fan of a yacht. Using leaked documents, Forbes counted 16 belonging to the Russian oligarch. My ship location app tells me that the superest of his fleet – Solaris (140-metres) and Eclipse (162-metres), both registered in the Cook Islands – are now parked in the Sea of Marmara, near Istanbul. When western governments seized Russian oligarchs’ assets after the invasion of Ukraine, Turkey refused to join the sanctions and became a bolt-hole.

Eclipse doesn’t even eclipse everything. The world’s longest superyacht, at 180-metres, is Azzam, launched in 2013 for Sheikh Khalifa bin Zayed Al Nahyan of Abu Dhabi, who died in 2022, but according to Boat International and the Superyacht Fan website , Azzam is still in the family. When you get to this level it’s not always clear who owns a yacht, as they can be held in trusts or shell companies, sometimes across several jurisdictions.

Take Dilbar for example – a little shorter than Azzam but the world’s largest by volume. In June Bloomberg reported that a court in Germany had ruled that sanctions no longer applied to the yacht after finding insufficient evidence that the Russian billionaire Alisher Usmanov controls The Sister Trust, which formally owns the vessel.

Or Kosatka, formerly Graceful, the 82-metre yacht seen being escorted through Danish waters by Russian naval vessels in the summer and widely reported to be linked to Vladimir Putin. A bigger, 140-metre yacht, the €620m Scheherazade, which boasts two helipads, anti-drone technology and a cryotherapy room, remains impounded in Italy. Activists working for poisoned Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny believe that one is also owned by Putin.

T here is no secret about who owns the aptly named Leviathan, the biggest boat at the Monaco Yacht Show. Co-founder and president of the video game company Valve, Gabe Newell doesn’t just own the 111-metre Leviathan, he also owns the 93-metre support vessel Draak, parked up next door.

I am allowed on to Leviathan and get a brief look around. I’m shown the huge mess area, which Newell and his guests share with the 42 crew. As well as the pool, there’s an outdoor cinema, basketball court, and a huge gaming lounge with consoles and race simulators, open to everyone. The crew are also keen to point out Leviathan’s diesel-electric hybrid propulsion and battery energy storage system. But it still has a 494,000-litre fuel tank. Fill ’er up? Certainly sir, that’ll be roughly a million euros.

It’s not total eco denial at the Monaco Yacht Show however, there’s at least some acknowledgment of environmental impact. I drop in on the Blue Wake awards, “for solutions delivering measurable impact on yachting sustainability”. So there’s a prize for a company using more sustainable materials for yacht interiors. A yacht wins a Blue Wake for having sails, and a marina gets one for planting Posidonia plants.

This is all good news … but actually, when you look at it, it’s not that good. In five years 3,000 sq metres of Posidonia have been restored – sounds impressive, but then by my calculations that’s an area of about 55 metres by 55 metres. The boat with sails? Great, but actually there are fewer sailing boats here than in previous years, the trend is towards power, more and more of it.

It looks like greenwashing, token gestures. I have an Italian friend who calls these superyachts stronzi di mare – turds of the sea. And you know what you can’t do to a turd. There’s no escaping the truth: that they drink fossil fuels like there’s no tomorrow, which there won’t be if they’re allowed to carry on; that there’s no more monstrous symbol of inequality; and that they look like irons.

But before storming off in disgust, maybe I’ll just pop into that wine tasting. In my socks.

stories.body:
More than 8,900 people aged under 30 were arrested for money laundering offences in England and Wales between 2020 and 2025. That’s more than six in ten of all money laundering arrests recorded during the period.

And our analysis of police data points to a growing problem that is not simply about young people committing financial crime . It also reveals how organised crime groups are recruiting young people as “money mules”. These are people who move or receive criminal funds on behalf of others.

The UK government already recognises the threat posed by money mule networks. The 2025 national risk assessment identified schools and universities as an emerging risk.

Students appear to be particularly vulnerable. The police officers we interviewed for our report said young people can be targeted because they may be under financial pressure, lack experience in managing money or be unaware of the risks of becoming involved in money laundering. International students were considered especially vulnerable, with officers reporting that some are targeted soon after arriving in the UK.

A money mule may be asked to receive funds into their bank account and transfer it elsewhere, sometimes in return for payment. They may not realise where the money came from or understand that what they are doing is a criminal offence.

Our analysis of data obtained from 36 police forces through freedom of information requests found 14,493 money laundering arrests between January 2020 and January 2025. Of these, 8,956 involved people aged 18 to 29. A further 776 under-18s were recorded by 35 forces.

These figures do not tell us how many of those arrested were students. Police forces do not routinely record student status, so age is only an imperfect indication of involvement in education. But the scale of youth involvement is clear.

Students are vulnerable to acting as a money mules because they face financial pressures, are engaged with social media and lack awareness of the legal consequences of acting as a money mule. Organised crime groups have exploited these factors by using fake job advertisements and online recruitment tactics that promise easy income in exchange for using personal bank accounts to transfer funds.

International students may be especially vulnerable due to their need for UK bank accounts and cross-border financial activity. As a result, students can become unwitting participants in laundering the proceeds of fraud and organised crime. As one police officer told us “as soon as international students land in the UK … they are inundated with messages about money laundering”.

The data also reveals large differences between police forces. Money laundering arrests were concentrated in some of the UK’s largest urban areas. However, this may reflect differences in the scale of organised crime, financial activity and police resources. It may also reflect differences in how forces record offences.

More broadly, our report suggests that the criminal justice system is better equipped to deal with relatively straightforward money laundering cases than the more complex networks behind them. This is important because focusing on the person who moves the money can obscure the people directing the operation.

Read more: Money laundering plays a key role in every part of the illegal drugs industry – here’s how it works

Young people recruited as money mules may be involved at the lowest level of a much larger criminal enterprise. Some may knowingly participate. Others may be manipulated , exploited or persuaded that what they are doing is harmless.

Our report noted that universities can be exposed to money laundering in a number of ways including through payments of fees or donations – thus unknowingly facilitating money laundering by students.

Yet universities are not currently covered by the UK’s money laundering regulations 2017 in the same way as regulated sectors such as banks, lawyers and accountants. That means universities do not have the same general obligations to identify and report suspected money laundering.

Our previous research illustrated that universities are susceptible to money laundering due to large financial flows and receipt of cash payments for tuition and accommodation fees. That research also found that over 20% of universities do not provide any anti-money laundering guidance to their students.

In our interviews and surveys with regional organised crime units and the City of London Police, we found uncertainty about how the rules apply to higher education. This can leave police focusing on the person receiving or transferring illicit money, rather than on potential risks within the institution or the wider criminal network.

An inconsistency problem

Police interviewees described shortages of staff, specialist expertise and investigative resources. Some said economic crime could become a forgotten area when police forces are dealing with competing priorities.

Relationships between police forces and universities also varied considerably. In some areas, there were established local contacts and effective partnerships. In others, cooperation depended on individual relationships rather than a consistent national approach.

This fragmented response is particularly problematic when criminal networks operate across police force boundaries.

Read more: Successive UK governments keep failing on fraud – and the problem is only getting worse

Our analysis does not suggest that universities are routinely being used to launder money. Nor can it establish how many students are involved in recorded money laundering offences. The available data has limitations, including differences in how police forces record offences.

But our findings point to a clear gap between the scale of the problem and the information available about it.

What should happen next?

Our analysis points to four priorities.

First, universities should be brought within the money laundering regulations. This would give higher education institutions clear responsibilities for identifying and reporting suspected money laundering.

Second, prevention needs to start earlier and be more targeted. Universities should include money-mule awareness in student induction programmes, alongside financial education and social media campaigns. International students, who may be unfamiliar with the risks and the UK banking system, should receive particular support.

Read more: Universities and their students are vulnerable to money laundering – new research

Third, universities and police forces need stronger partnerships. Sharing information and building established links could help identify suspicious activity and patterns of recruitment before individual cases become part of a larger criminal investigation.

Finally, the Home Office should develop a dedicated national strategy for money laundering and money-mule activity in educational settings. A consistent approach would help address the uneven enforcement, resources and relationships between police forces that our report identified.

Our report suggests that tackling money laundering effectively means looking beyond the person whose bank account receives the money. Young people may be the most visible part of the problem. But they are not necessarily the ones at the heart of it.
